groups.title: Redis Data Structures
groups.question: Explain how you would use Redis in an API, and how you pick the right data structure for the job.

followUps.Strings, Hashes & TTL Expiry: When would you store data in a hash instead of a string, and what happens if cached keys never get a TTL?
followUps.Sorted Sets for Rate Limiting & Leaderbo: How would a sorted set help you build a leaderboard or a sliding-window rate limiter?

evidence.text: A hash stores the fields of one object, so one field can be read or updated without rewriting the whole value.
A TTL makes a cached key expire on its own.
Without TTLs memory grows until maxmemory, and then writes fail or the eviction policy drops keys you still need.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Redis, hash, TTL) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Redis removes old keys by itself even without a TTL.

evidence.text: A sorted set keeps members ordered by a score, so top-N and rank lookups are fast.
For a leaderboard the score is the player's points.
For a sliding-window limiter the score is the request time: drop entries older than the window and count the rest.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (sorted set, ZADD) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a sorted set is a plain list that gets sorted when you read it.

groups.title: HTTP Caching
groups.question: Explain how HTTP caching works between your API, a CDN and the browser, and how you control it.

followUps.Cache-Control Directives & CDN Interacti: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store, and which one should a response with private user data use?
followUps.ETag & Conditional Requests: How does an ETag let a client avoid downloading the same response again?

evidence.text: no-store means the response must not be kept anywhere.
no-cache means it may be stored but must be revalidated with the server before each reuse.
Private user data should use no-store (or at least private), so shared caches and the browser don't keep it.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (no-cache, no-store, max-age) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says no-cache means the response is never stored.

evidence.text: An ETag identifies one version of a response.
The client sends it back in an If-None-Match header.
If nothing changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body and the client reuses its copy.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (ETag, 304) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the ETag is the response's expiry time.

groups.title: Application-Level Caching
groups.question: Explain how you would add a cache in front of your database, and what makes it hard to get right.

followUps.Cache-Aside Pattern & Invalidation: Walk through a cache-aside read. What must happen to the cached copy when the data in the database changes?
followUps.N+1 Query Problem & the DataLoader Patte: Fetching 100 books and their authors runs 101 queries. Why, and how do you get it down to 2?

evidence.text: Read the cache first; on a miss, read the database and write the result into the cache.
When the data changes, delete or update the cached copy, and/or rely on a TTL.
Otherwise readers keep getting stale data that looks just as valid as fresh data.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (cache-aside, invalidation) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the database updates the cache automatically when the data changes.

evidence.text: One query loads the list, then one more query runs per item, so 100 books cost 101 queries.
Load all the related rows in one query instead: WHERE id IN (...), a join, or a batching loader like DataLoader.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (N+1, DataLoader) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the fix is adding more database connections.

groups.title: Response Optimization
groups.question: Explain how you would make large API responses faster and cheaper to send.

followUps.gzip & Brotli Compression: How does the server know a client can accept a compressed response?
followUps.Pagination — Offset vs Cursor: Why does offset pagination get slower on deep pages, and how does cursor pagination avoid that?

evidence.text: The client sends Accept-Encoding, listing the formats it can decompress, such as gzip or br.
The server compresses only with a listed format and says which one in Content-Encoding.
Text like JSON shrinks a lot, so much less data is sent.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (gzip, Brotli) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the server compresses every response no matter what the client accepts.

evidence.text: With OFFSET the database still reads and throws away all the skipped rows, so deep pages get slower and slower.
Cursor pagination remembers the last item's key and asks for the rows after it, like WHERE id > last_id.
That jumps straight to the right spot through an index, so every page costs about the same.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (offset, cursor, pagination) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says offset is slow on deep pages only because the response is bigger.
